## Discussion

In this randomized placebo‑controlled trial of a WBI for individuals who committed CSA or CSEM offences, no superiority of the intervention arm compared to the placebo arm was observed. Among secondary outcomes, only some risk factors showed significant changes in the intervention arm in line with the hypotheses, most notably a reduced sexual interest in children. Also in line with our hypothesis, treatment readiness was enhanced in the intervention arm. Against the hypothesis, difficulties in emotion regulations increased significantly in the intervention arm, whereas the perceived social support increased isolated in the placebo arm. Only in the intervention arm, post-hoc analyses demonstrated robust significant improvements in the working alliance with STs and SOs. No evidence emerged for an increased risk of recidivism. The frequency of adverse events was generally low without significant differences between trial arms.

The overall null effect is in line with recent meta-analyses considering in-face treatment programs showing that studies with high methodological quality tend to report smaller or null effects. [@holperModeratorsSexualRecidivism2024; @olverSexualOffenseTreatment2025] Nevertheless, the result contrasts to the only other placebo‑controlled evaluation of a WBI study in a comparable population, which reported a small, but significant effect in favor of the intervention arm on reducing the amount viewing CSEM [@latthEffectsInternetdeliveredCognitive2022]. Conceptually, the current WBI differs substantially from the WBI in this study, mainly regarding complexity, intensity, and the studied sample, questioning comparability. Previous evidence suggests that higher treatment intensity is generally associated with larger effects [@olverSexualOffenseTreatment2025], yet this relationship did not translate into superior outcomes in the present WBI failing possibly due to a too low baseline risk of our sample. Also dropout rates were high, reports on adverse events were generally low in both RCTs (in Lätth et al. even lower than in the placebo arm). For the first time, our study provides evidence that this also holds true for individuals, who already committed CSA or CSEM offences.

Several mechanisms may underlie the null findings on the primary outcome. Dropout may have been driven in part by participants’ interest in receiving official documentation for court rather than financial compensation resulting in low protocol adherence and motivation. Moreover, baseline levels of several secondary outcomes risk factors were low, suggesting a violation of the need principle of the RNR model by not adapting the content of the WBI based on these baseline characteristics. [@andrewsPsychologyCriminalConduct2010] Only module five provided individualized treatment content, but failed to show a significant reduction of offense-supportive conditions. Meta‑analyses indicate that programs targeting high‑risk individuals and relevant needs yield larger effects. [@holperModeratorsSexualRecidivism2024; @olverSexualOffenseTreatment2025] Overall, our study was underpowered to detect small effects, as the predefined sample size was not reached. Furthermore, it was not possible to recruit a representative sample of all individuals on probation in Germany due to restricted access and data protection regulations. Financial compensation was provided to reduce potential volunteer bias, but selective referral by probation officers cannot be ruled out. Also, engaging with the WBI necessitated an ability to read German, which is not available to everyone. At the same time, to our knowledge, this is the first randomized placebo controlled clinical trial of an WBI in Germany recruiting participants from almost all federal states and seems to be the RCT with the highest sample size until now. Lack of direct contact with participants during the intervention limited participation retention efforts, as reminders could only be communicated via SOs. Many participants failed to complete the modules within the advised time, which likely contributed to premature study termination. Participants in the intervention arm consistently required more time to complete modules than recommended and more time than participants in the placebo arm. Although differences were attenuated after correction for multiple testing, this prolonged duration may have compromised comparability at later assessments and contributed to dropout. Another explanation for the null effect may be the predominance of low‑risk individuals in the sample. Sthe score on secondary endpoints suggest that many participants scored within normal ranges, indicating limited severity of risk factors. Also, psychological burden in the sample was low, which contrasts with previous literature reporting substantial psychological distress among individuals with sexual interest in children and high rates of paraphilias. [@chronosTreatmentNeedsExperiences2024; @latthChildSexualAbuse2025] The divergent results may be based in the fact, that the rate of self-reported pedophilic disorders is lower in the current sample and all participants have already been convicted. Lastly, officially recorded re-offenses are considered the gold standard outcome measure and self‑reports are controversial discussed, recent evidence suggests that self‑reported data can be informative regarding recidivism risk. [@mcmahanPredictiveAbilitySexual2026] Nevertheless, the CARES is a new instrument, and data linking it to official recidivism outcomes are not yet available. [@sonjaetzlerDevelopmentInitialValidationsubmitted]

Sexual interest in children is considered as the most influencial risk factor for sexual recidivism. [@setoEmpiricallybasedDynamicRisk2023] A central controversy concerns the modifiability of sexual interests in children. While the current clinical paradigm assumes limited changeability, this remains an active scientific debate. Recent meta-analyses reported indications of treatment‑related changes in sexual interest, although none of the included studies employed an adequate control group. [@beggschristoffersonArousalManagementTechniques2026; @mcphailInterventionsPedohebephilicArousal2020] Against this background, the present trial provides further evidence for a possible reduction of sexual interest in children by treatment, compared to a matched control group. However, the magnitude of change was small, warranting cautious interpretation of the clinical significance.

Also in line with our hypothesis, treatment readiness was enhanced in the intervention arm. Against the hypothesis, difficulties in emotion regulations increased significantly in the intervention arm, whereas the perceived social support increased isolated in the placebo arm. Post-hoc analyses demonstrated robust significant improvements in the working alliance with both STs and SOs in the intervention arm.

:::

Future research should include in-face and waiting‑list control groups to clarify the relative effectiveness of the WBI. Especially revision of module three, a stricter RNR‑based individualization, and the integration of the WBI in a blended approaches into regular in-face treatment programs may enhance adherence and effectivity. From a more clinical and policy perspective, the findings underline the care gap in Germany, since baseline characteristics showed that most participants with court‑ordered treatment were not receiving in-face psychotherapy. Caution remain against recommending existing WBIs for individuals who committed CSA or CSEM offenses without rigorous evaluation: the observed increase of difficulties with regulations highlights the necessity of rigorous evaluation prior to implementation.
